To form the past subjunctive: avoir / être in the subjunctive + past participle (que j’aie fini, qu’elle soit née).

Thursday, 4 March, 7 a.m. The maternity ward of the Croix-Rousse hospital. Rose-Hélène was born during the night, at 3 o’clock, six days early. Hélène and Madame Bernard are the first visitors.
So? Where is she? I’m so glad everything went well!
She’s asleep, there, in the cot. Three kilos two hundred, fifty centimetres. And she yelled louder than Radu at our wedding.
(she slowly approaches the cot) Oh… How small she is. I can’t believe you gave her my name.
Would you like to hold her?
Me? But… I’ve never held a newborn. I wouldn’t want her to wake up.
Come on, Hélène. Sit down. I’ll show you. I held thousands of them when I was a doctor.
(holding the baby, moved) Hello, Rose-Hélène. Welcome to the world. I’m so happy you arrived before my eighty-sixth birthday.
It’s the most beautiful day I’ve ever lived. Even though I haven’t slept for thirty hours.
You haven’t slept? What about me, then? (she laughs) I’m sorry you were so frightened, though. You were paler than the doctors.
Fathers are always paler than mothers. Henri fainted when Isabelle was born. A nurse had to look after him for an hour.
(she laughs softly) That doesn’t surprise me. He was always afraid of hospitals.
And the families? I sent photos to Annecy and Iași. My mother replied within ten seconds with thirty hearts.
And Mum called me at four in the morning. She said Granny had taken the coach last night, even before I got to the hospital. She had “felt” it was time.
Your grandmother is incredible. She may well be in Hungary by now.
(very softly, to the baby) You see, little one? You’re barely three hours old, and already a whole family is crossing Europe for you.

“Kuh zhay”: the subjunctive of avoir sounds exactly like “j’ai”. Only the spelling (aie) is different.
“Kel swa nay”: three short, linked syllables.
“Noo-vo-nay”: stress on the last syllable. Plural: les nouveau-nés.
“A-koosh-mã”: the middle e disappears. The verb: accoucher = “a-koo-shay”.
It’s formed like the passé composé, but with the auxiliary in the PRESENT SUBJUNCTIVE: que j’aie / que je sois + past participle.
Same rules as the passé composé: verbs of movement and reflexive verbs take être, and the participle agrees: “que tout se soit bien passé”, “qu’elle soit arrivée”.
The choice depends on WHEN the action in the subjunctive clause happens, compared with the main verb:
Je suis contente qu’elle ait dormi.
Je suis heureuse que tu viennes.
Je suis heureuse que tu sois venu.
English has no past subjunctive in everyday use, so French “Je suis content que tu sois venu” corresponds to a simple “I’m glad you came”.
I’m so glad everything went well.

After a superlative (le plus, le meilleur, le seul, le premier, le dernier) + qui / que, French often uses the subjunctive, especially when expressing a personal opinion:
It’s the most beautiful day I’ve ever lived.
You’re the only person who can help me.
It’s a sign of elegant French. In relaxed speech, many French people use the indicative (“le plus beau jour que j’ai vécu”), but the subjunctive sounds much nicer.

In France, a birth must be registered at the town hall within 5 days. The parents then send friends a “faire-part de naissance”: a card with the baby’s name, date, time, weight and length.

On Wednesday 3 March, Julien was giving his pupils’ spring concert in the small hall of the conservatoire. Ioana hadn’t wanted to miss it, although the doctor had advised her to rest. “It’s the first time Théo is playing in public,” she had said. “I want to be there.”

She was sitting in the front row, with Madame Bernard on one side and Radu on the other. Lucia had come too, with a bouquet for Théo. The hall was full of proud parents, moved grandparents and bored little brothers.
Théo went up on stage, very pale, in a black suit. He sat down at the piano, looked at Julien, and began to play Henri’s waltz. Ioana smiled. It was the piece she loved most in the world.

It was in the middle of the second verse that she felt the first contraction. She squeezed Madame Bernard’s hand. The former doctor turned her head, looked Ioana in the eyes, and understood at once. She looked at her watch.

“We’ll wait for the end of the waltz,” she whispered. “That little boy has to finish his piece. Then we’ll go.” Ioana nodded, her teeth clenched. Théo played to the very last note, without a single mistake. The audience applauded. So did Ioana, breathing very hard.

When Julien saw Madame Bernard stand up and signal to him, he understood too. He left his pupils with a colleague, ran to Ioana, and knocked over two chairs crossing the hall. The parents thought it was part of the show.

Radu called a taxi. Lucia took the bag Ioana had packed two weeks earlier, just in case. Madame Bernard gave the driver instructions like a general. And at ten in the evening they arrived at the Croix-Rousse maternity ward, two streets from home.

The night was long. Very long. Radu and Lucia waited in the corridor, sitting on plastic chairs. Madame Bernard had gone home after making sure everything was fine, but she phoned every hour. Nobody slept.

In the delivery room, Julien held Ioana’s hand. Between two contractions he took out his phone and played the recording of the lullaby he had composed. The midwife, a woman in her sixties with a strong Marseille accent, smiled. “Did you write that? It’s very beautiful. Babies like music, you know.”

At twelve minutes past three in the morning, on Thursday 4 March, Rose-Hélène Moreau was born. She cried straight away, very loudly, as if to tell the whole world she had arrived. The midwife laid her on Ioana’s chest.

Ioana looked at that little red, wrinkled face, those tiny hands, that black hair stuck to her head. She wasn’t crying. She was just smiling, unable to stop. “Hello, my little one. Hello, Rose-Hélène. I’m so happy you’re here.”
Julien, on the other hand, was crying like a child. He couldn’t speak. He just touched his daughter’s tiny hand with the tip of his finger. And the tiny hand closed around his finger, very tightly.
In the corridor, Radu had fallen asleep on Lucia’s shoulder. When Julien came out, his eyes red and a huge smile on his face, Lucia gently shook Radu. “Radu! Wake up! You’re an uncle!”
Radu leapt to his feet, hugged Julien, then Lucia, then a nurse who happened to be passing and hadn’t asked for anything. Then he took out his phone. “I have to call Mum! Right now!”

It was four in the morning in Lyon, five in Iași. Elena answered on the first ring. She wasn’t asleep either. “It’s a girl, Mum! Three kilos two hundred! Everyone’s fine!” At the other end of the line there was a scream, then tears, then Dan’s voice shouting too, in the background.

“And Granny?” asked Radu. “You have to tell her!” Elena laughed through her tears. “Your grandmother? She isn’t here. Last night at eight she picked up her bag and went to the coach station. She said she had felt the baby was coming. She’s been on the coach to Lyon since nine.”

Radu hung up, looked at Julien, and they both burst out laughing, exhausted and happy, in the middle of the silent maternity corridor. Somewhere between Romania and Hungary, an eighty-two-year-old lady was asleep on a coach, her head against the window, a smile on her lips. She already knew.

At six, Julien went home to feed Victor and pick up a few things. Rue d’Austerlitz was still dark and silent. Only Sophie’s bakery was lit. Through the window you could see her taking the first croissants out of the oven.

Julien knocked on the glass. Sophie looked up, saw his face, and understood before he even opened his mouth. She ran to open the door, her hands covered in flour. “Well? Well?” “A girl. Rose-Hélène. Three kilos two hundred.” Sophie kissed him, and he had flour on both cheeks all morning.

An hour later, when the first customers arrived, they found a big sheet of paper stuck to the bakery window. Sophie had written on it in red letters: “It’s a girl! Rose-Hélène, born last night. Free croissants for everyone this morning.”

Meanwhile, in Annecy, Pierre and Brigitte had already caught the first train. Brigitte had spent the night knitting a pink bonnet. Pierre had put in his bag the most beautiful brioche he had ever made, with his granddaughter’s name written in sugar. He had made it at three in the morning, exactly as she was being born, without knowing it.
That morning, the whole of Croix-Rousse learnt that a little girl had been born on rue d’Austerlitz. And Victor, who hadn’t understood a thing, ate two whole croissants.
